questions.question: D1 — Pass 1 (Getting Started): The agreed <2 min TTHW target is mathematically impossible with the retained 5-min CI block. Which resolution belongs in the plan? <gstack-qid:devex-d1-tthw-contradiction>

options.label: Demo-only CI bypass (Recommended)
options.description: Add an offline mode specifically for `python -m evalkit.demo`. The demo runs bundled sample_responses.json with no real API submission, so the CI check has nothing to gate. This achieves the <2 min target for the agreed first-success experience without touching the real API contract. Scope impact: small — only evalkit/demo.py changes.

options.label: Add --offline flag to run_eval
options.description: Give run_eval and run_batch an --offline=True flag that skips the CI block, enabling local dev testing. Achieves <2 min for both demo AND real usage in local mode. Broader fix, but expands scope beyond DX POLISH into API surface change.

options.label: Update TTHW target to reflect reality
options.description: Change the agreed target from <2 min to <7 min in the plan. No code change, no scope expansion. Honest about the current experience, but drops EvalKit below all three competitors (A=2min, B=4min, C=3min) and accepts the 'Needs Work' tier explicitly.

options.label: Other — describe the constraint
options.description: There's a constraint or design intent I haven't surfaced. Tell me what's actually going on with the CI block and the TTHW target.

questions.question: D2 — Pass 1+4 (Getting Started + Docs): The README tells developers to run `python examples/first_eval.py`, but docs/package-contents.txt explicitly states that file is absent from both the published package and the release examples archive. A developer's first command fails with FileNotFoundError. What's the fix? <gstack-qid:devex-d2-missing-quickstart>

options.label: Update README to point at the demo (Recommended)
options.description: Replace the `python examples/first_eval.py` instruction in README with `python -m evalkit.demo`. The demo module IS in the package, produces real scored output, and is the agreed first-success vehicle. Zero new files needed, one line changes in README.

options.label: Add first_eval.py to the package
options.description: Write examples/first_eval.py and include it in the package so the documented path works. More complete — developers have a real code file they can open and extend. But adds scope: file must be authored, tested, and maintained alongside demo.py.

options.label: Both: update README AND add the file
options.description: Update README to use the demo command as the primary path, AND add examples/first_eval.py as a secondary reference for developers who want editable starter code. Most complete. Two deliverables instead of one.

options.label: Other — first_eval.py is coming from somewhere else
options.description: The file exists or will exist in a place I haven't looked. Tell me where it is or where it's meant to come from.

answers.D2 \u2014 Pass 1+4 (Getting Started + Do: Update README to point at the demo (Recommended)

questions.question: D3 — Pass 3 (Error Messages): The SDK raises `AuthError("request failed")` for an invalid API key. No error code, no explanation of what failed, no instruction for how to fix it. The plan explicitly retains this message. An ML engineer with a typo in EVALKIT_API_KEY sees a two-word error and has no idea what broke. Fix or retain? <gstack-qid:devex-d3-autherror-message>

options.label: Fix the error message (Recommended)
options.description: Improve to: `AuthError("Authentication failed: EVALKIT_API_KEY is invalid or expired. Check your key at console.evalkit.com/keys and set the EVALKIT_API_KEY environment variable.")`. Follows DX First Principle #5: every error = problem + cause + fix. One-line change in evalkit/client.py.

options.label: Add error code only
options.description: Change to `AuthError("auth_invalid: request failed")` — adds a stable machine-readable code without restructuring the message. Useful for programmatic error handling but still leaves the developer without a cause or fix.

options.label: Retain the current message
options.description: Explicitly accept this as a known DX debt item. The plan notes it as a post-beta improvement. An ML engineer who hits this will need to consult docs or support to diagnose it.

questions.question: D4 — Pass 2 (API Design): `run_eval(dataset, evaluator)` and `run_batch(evaluator, dataset)` have REVERSED positional order for the same concepts. The plan calls this intentional. A developer who writes `run_eval(my_dataset, my_evaluator)` then calls `run_batch` the same way silently passes wrong types — no error until runtime, potentially confusing results. Fix or keep? <gstack-qid:devex-d4-argorder-reversal>

options.label: Standardize both to (dataset, evaluator) order (Recommended)
options.description: Change run_batch signature to `run_batch(dataset, evaluator)` in the beta. Consistent with run_eval, intuitive (dataset first, evaluator second), and v2 is a beta with breaking-change latitude. Fixes the cognitive trap before the API is widely adopted.

options.label: Enforce keyword-only arguments on both
options.description: Add `*` to both signatures: `run_eval(*, dataset, evaluator)` and `run_batch(*, evaluator, dataset)`. Callers must use keyword args; positional mistakes become TypeErrors immediately. Preserves the current positional order while making silent misuse impossible.

options.label: Retain reversed order, add prominent docs warning
options.description: Keep the current signatures and add a big warning box in the docs: 'Note: run_eval and run_batch take arguments in reversed order.' Accepts the cognitive trap but documents it. Lowest implementation cost.

options.label: Retain as intentional — it mirrors the underlying evaluator API convention
options.description: The reversal follows an existing convention in the underlying evaluator library. Document the rationale in the API reference so the design looks intentional, not accidental.

questions.question: D5 — Pass 5 (Upgrade Path): v1 exposed `Client.evaluate()`. v2 removes it immediately and replaces it with `Client.run()`. No alias, no deprecation warning, no migration guide, no codemod. Every existing v1 user who runs `pip install evalkit==2.0.0b1` and calls `Client.evaluate()` gets an `AttributeError` with no guidance. The plan retains this. What bridge should the beta include? <gstack-qid:devex-d5-v1v2-migration>

options.label: Deprecation alias + migration guide (Recommended)
options.description: Add `Client.evaluate = Client.run` with a DeprecationWarning: 'evaluate() is deprecated in v2; use run() instead.' Add one section to the changelog explaining the rename. The alias makes the upgrade non-breaking for v1 users; the warning tells them to update. Removes entirely in v3.

options.label: Migration guide only, no alias
options.description: Write a v1→v2 migration section in CHANGELOG.md (and/or README) documenting `evaluate()` → `run()`. No code change. Developers who read changelogs before upgrading are fine; developers who just run pip upgrade hit an AttributeError and must consult docs.

options.label: Hard break as-is, add clear error message
options.description: Keep the hard break but improve the AttributeError: catch `__getattr__` and raise a descriptive error: `AttributeError: Client.evaluate() was renamed to Client.run() in v2. See CHANGELOG.md.` The developer knows exactly what to do, no alias needed.

options.label: Retain as-is — it's a beta, accept the break
options.description: Beta users accept breaking changes. The changelog mentions it. Developers who upgrade without reading the changelog chose to take the risk. No additional bridge needed.
